reuse.raw: The local GenBank flat-file snapshot is ignored and not included in version control; no nucleotide sequence or source table is copied into the tracked review.
reuse.content: NCBI says it places no general restrictions on GenBank data use but notes submitters may claim intellectual-property rights and NCBI cannot grant them. Wiley's publisher page displayed no article-specific open license and said the hosted full text was unavailable; its terms do not grant public republication rights. No item-specific redistribution or public-app approval is inferred.

caveats: The article abstract reports 118 individuals and 23 species, while the reviewed HQ654 range contains 113 records and 23 GenBank organism annotations. Five separately retrieved HQ231 Sardinella tawilis accessions also cite the article and a second paper; their sample linkage is unresolved and they are not added as another taxon.

All 113 core records have source locality text, date, voucher and identifier metadata, but all also contain a lat_lon field. Eighty-eight coordinates fall outside a broad nonofficial plausibility envelope; the other 25 were not validated against exact localities. Withhold every coordinate from this batch.

The Catalog of Fishes crosswalk maps Apogon hyalosoma to Yarica hyalosoma and reports Oxudercidae for Oligolepis acutipennis; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy reports Gobiidae for that same species. The family conflict remains unresolved. The crosswalk validates nomenclature only, not sequenced-specimen identity.

Wiley's full article and specimen documentation were unavailable in the reviewed publisher page, and no article-specific open license was identified. This is historical molecular specimen metadata, not current presence, abundance, catchability, natural diet, legal access, safety, or a complete Taal Lake checklist.

access.status: Official NFRDI journal and repository records plus the official article PDF's indexed full-text extraction were reviewed. reuse.raw: No paper PDF, table image, photograph, extended prose or voucher image copied into the repository.

caveats: The combined eight-taxon list draws from fisher catch and a 21-person non-probability interview; Table 2 records only five taxa in fishers' catches, totaling 1,462 individuals. Do not label all eight as specimen-caught in the study.

A 2021 conference abstract reports four taxa and 475 fish during a period nested within the later paper's sampling window. Author overlap and timing indicate possible shared project/data, but no sample-level crosswalk proves independence or exact overlap; never add these totals as separate evidence.

Names, native/introduced status, introduction years, local names and gear associations are transcribed as the authors report them. They have not been independently taxonomically or historically validated; the paper's table and narrative give different introduction timelines for Oreochromis niloticus.

The study is based on subsistence fishers' daily catches and interviews, not standardized effort across all lake habitats. It does not establish current occupancy, lake-wide abundance, complete species coverage or catchability.
The article's Lake Danao coordinates are a study-area locator, not species-specific stations; the datum is not stated and no point or lake geometry is generated.

Diet discussion for Glossogobius giuris and Cyprinus carpio includes cited literature and/or fisher observations; it is not a dedicated local diet study and is not approved as a Bangwit diet or bait recommendation.
The article's CC BY-NC 4.0 terms restrict reuse to attributed noncommercial purposes. No Bangwit publication approval or commercial-use right is established.

reuse.content: The article states copyright © National University of Singapore; no open license or public-app reuse permission was verified. Retain only concise attributed research notes pending rights review.

caveats: The material list enumerates 16 paratypes, while Table 1 says the measurements cover 14 paratypes; the article does not reconcile this count.
The original paper names Babuyan in its distribution statement but does not list a Babuyan specimen in the material examined section.
The Iwahig record was identified as Cyclocheilichthys armatus by an earlier source; the authors had not examined it and only hypothesized it might be this species.
The 2025 checklist prints schopeae, a spelling variant, and reports that WPU-PPC staff could not confirm whether its type specimens were deposited there.
The official IUCN search result indicates Endangered based on an assessment last assessed in 2020, but direct assessment access returned HTTP 403; no fine-scale locality was retained.
Three non-type stomach samples are not a complete diet profile and do not support bait recommendations.

caveats: The extracted records are synthesized species–drainage-basin associations, not dated specimen or observation events.

Twenty-nine listed basins are labeled Philippines-only; Sandakan and Sulu are shared-country basin rows that also include Malaysia and must not be treated as Philippines-only.
The 31 represented basin rows are not a complete inventory of Philippine basins or surface waters.
The dataset has no native/introduced status field and broad basin associations may include brackish or marine-influenced taxa.

All 31 extracted per-basin unique-name counts reconcile to the basin attribute n_specs values in the same Zenodo record. This is an internal file-consistency check, not independent validation of taxonomy, geometry, or local species presence.

The workbook defines referenceIds as Catalogue of Fishes bibliography for species descriptions or taxonomic assignments, not as basin-specific citations; underlying studies still require independent review before any species–basin link is used.

The B0380 Cagayan polygon is a northern Luzon drainage-basin feature; it is not an administrative boundary or municipal-water limit. The accompanying bounded GBIF screen does not make the basin candidate list exhaustive.
No public species or occurrence rows, diet, bait, catchability, legal, safety, or waterbody geometry claims are admitted from this extract.

caveats: The paper reports random fish specimens from cooperating fishers' catches at landing sites; the table does not provide a taxon-by-sampling-site or taxon-by-event crosswalk.
BFAR restoration and fingerling/breeder interventions were reported before/during the study era; the fish paper does not identify stocked individuals or list the taxa stocked.

Six table percentages do not match standard two-decimal recalculation from the reported counts; the abstract's Oreochromis niloticus percentage also differs from its table. The authors describe the single Acanthopagrus latus as transient from nearby brackish Buguey Lagoon; do not classify it as an established freshwater resident from this record.
No article-level reuse license was found in searchable PDF text; this bounded check does not establish the full legal status of the work.

reuse.metadata: Cite Lausan et al. (2023), journal, volume, issue, pages, and publisher article page.
reuse.raw: No PDF, tables, figures, specimen images, or raw data copied into the repository.
reuse.content: Only brief attributed study-scope, method, site-label, and sample-count notes are retained for research triage. No public-app projection or table redistribution is approved.

sources.license: The article page gives conflicting item-level statements: CC BY-NC 4.0 in Paper Details and CC BY 4.0 in its Copyright Information section. Treat article and data reuse as uncleared until the publisher or authors resolve the conflict.
caveats: The article reports 308 M. anguillicaudatus from three rice-field/terrace stations in Bauko, Bontoc, and Tadian, sampled weekly from late December 2022 to late February 2023; counts are not abundance or catch-rate estimates.
The paper calls station coordinates approximate but does not state how they were derived, their datum, or spatial uncertainty.
The reviewed methods do not state a species-identification procedure and provide no specimen accession number or repository; the author-reported name is not independently verified.
The article's abstract, station 2 narrative/table, and male length-weight exponent contain internal numerical discrepancies; do not ingest the biological metrics without clarification.
The paper separately cites a 2019 pond-culture study in Bauko; pond-culture records must not be merged with wild rice-field evidence or generalized to rivers and lakes.
No diet, current presence, legal catchability, season rule, water safety, or complete Mountain Province fish list can be inferred from this study.

The samples were from fish ponds; they do not establish a wild river/lake population, legal catchability, current presence, or a province-wide distribution.

sources.provider: Alexander N. Urquhart and Peter Koetsier; Western North American Naturalist; Boise State University ScholarWorks
sources.role: Peer-reviewed primary stomach-content study of an introduced Idaho population; supports a geographically bounded diet observation, not Philippine diet or occurrence.
sources.citation: Urquhart, A. N., & Koetsier, P. (2014). Diet of a cryptic but widespread invader, the oriental weatherfish (Misgurnus anguillicaudatus) in Idaho, USA. Western North American Naturalist, 74(1), 92-98. https://doi.org/10.3398/064.074.0109.

reuse.metadata: Cite Urquhart and Koetsier (2014), Western North American Naturalist, 74(1), 92-98, DOI 10.3398/064.074.0109, and the Boise State ScholarWorks item page.
reuse.raw: No PDF, table, figure, or individual stomach-content data copied into the repository.
reuse.content: Only a concise attributed summary of repository metadata and the abstract is retained. The item page identifies the work as CC BY 3.0; no article content is reproduced.

sources.license: Boise State ScholarWorks item page identifies this work as available under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0.
caveats: The authors sampled 237 fish from water bodies connected to the Boise River, Idaho, using baited minnow traps; 158 stomachs were empty, 42 contained only trap bait, and 37 contained natural food items.
The abstract reports macroinvertebrates as the primary diet component and chironomid larvae as the most numerous prey; detritus is described as likely important based on graphical analysis.
The high empty/bait-only stomach counts and baited capture method limit generalization; the sample represents an introduced population in Idaho, not a Philippine population.
Do not use this study alone to publish Philippine prey claims, fish-eating behavior, bait advice, local catchability, or legal guidance.

sources.title: Ecology of the Japanese Loach, Misgurnus anguillicaudatus (Cantor) (II): Food Habit
sources.provider: Zenziro Kubota; National Fisheries University; Yamaguchi Prefecture institutional repository
sources.role: Primary historical native-range diet study using gut-content observations from Nagata River, Japan; not Philippine diet, current population, or bait evidence.
sources.citation: Kubota, Zenziro. (1961). Ecology of the Japanese Loach, Misgurnus anguillicaudatus (Cantor) (II): Food Habit. Journal of National Fisheries University, 11(1), 177-195.

reuse.metadata: Cite Kubota (1961), Journal of National Fisheries University, 11(1), 177-195, and the Yamaguchi Prefectural University repository record.
reuse.raw: No PDF, figure, table, or transcribed individual gut-content data copied into the repository.
reuse.content: Only concise attributed method and finding summaries are retained. Repository metadata says open access but no item-specific redistribution license was verified.

sources.license: Repository labels the version of record open access; no item-specific Creative Commons or redistribution license verified.
caveats: The article reports gut-content samples collected in 1958-1959 from Nagata River, Shimonoseki, Japan, with body lengths of 15-131 mm; this is a historical single-river sample, not Philippine evidence.

The author describes size-related diet change, including animal plankton/invertebrates in smaller fish and increasing plant material, especially Spirogyra, in larger fish; the summary calls adults essentially herbivorous but notes temporary carnivory after spawning.
The paper's methods use coarse microscopic abundance codes; a single total sample denominator and modern voucher or molecular identity check were not found in the reviewed record and methods.
Season, body size and local food availability matter; the findings do not support an absolute species-wide diet label, prey list for the Philippines, bait advice, catchability or legal guidance.

sources.role: Primary native-range field study of occurrence and stomach contents in rice-field irrigation drainages; its diet sample is a July co-occurrence subset, not a year-round or Philippine diet dataset.
sources.citation: Kanou, K., Saito, S., Fuchigami, S., Imamura, A., Imai, H., & Taki, Y. (2007). Occurrence Patterns and Food Habits of Introduced Alien Loach Paramisgurnus dabryanus and Native Loach Misgurnus anguillicaudatus at Irrigation Drainages around Rice Fields in the Watarase River System, Central Honshu, Japan. Aquaculture Science, 55(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.11233/aquaculturesci1953.55.109.

reuse.metadata: Cite Kanou et al. (2007), Aquaculture Science, 55(1), 109-114, DOI 10.11233/aquaculturesci1953.55.109, and the J-STAGE article page.
reuse.raw: No PDF, table, figure, or individual stomach-content data copied into the repository.
reuse.content: Only concise attributed summaries of study scope and abstract/PDF findings are retained; no public-app diet projection is approved.

sources.license: J-STAGE identifies the item as a free journal article; no item-specific redistribution license was verified.
caveats: The study reports 3023 M. anguillicaudatus captured across January 2005-January 2006, but stomach contents for diet analysis were examined for 121 native loaches in the July 2005 co-occurrence sample.

The authors report ostracods, aquatic insect larvae, and Branchinella kugenumaensis as major foods; ostracods were eaten mainly below 30 mm standard length, while larger fish more often ate insect larvae and/or Branchinella.
Diet evidence concerns a Japanese rice-field drainage network and one July period; it does not establish prey use in Philippine rivers, lakes, rice fields, or other seasons.
Identification is author-reported and morphological; no specimen accession or molecular cross-check was reported in the reviewed article.
The paper compares diets with a similar co-occurring introduced loach, but it does not report M. anguillicaudatus eating fish. Do not turn diet overlap into a predator claim or bait advice.

Do not copy the article's diet table, percentages, or figures. No app row or derivative diet dataset is approved while license notices conflict.

sources.title: Synopsis of the biological data on dolphin-fishes, Coryphaena hippurus Linnaeus and Coryphaena equiselis Linnaeus
sources.provider: Barbara Jayne Palko, Grant L. Beardsley, and William J. Richards; NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service; FAO Fisheries Synopsis
sources.role: 1982 NOAA/FAO synthesis used to audit a secondary Batanes dolphinfish-diet citation. Its stomach-content summaries are from North Carolina, Gulf Stream, and other non-Philippine samples; they provide historical biological context, not Batanes-specific diet evidence or bait advice.
sources.citation: Palko, B. J., Beardsley, G. L., & Richards, W. J. (1982). Synopsis of the biological data on dolphin-fishes, Coryphaena hippurus Linnaeus and Coryphaena equiselis Linnaeus. NOAA Technical Report NMFS Circular 443; FAO Fisheries Synopsis No. 130.

reuse.metadata: NOAA repository identifies the technical report as Public Domain; cite the authors, 1982 title, NOAA Technical Report NMFS Circular 443, and FAO Fisheries Synopsis No. 130.
reuse.raw: No PDF or source figure was retained in the project.
reuse.content: Only concise attributed research notes are recorded. No figure, table, or adapted content was copied; publication approval remains false.

sources.license: Public Domain according to NOAA Institutional Repository metadata.
caveats: The report synthesizes studies across places, methods, and life stages; it is not a Batanes or Philippine feeding study.

Its nearly 25% flyingfish figure refers to the relative weight of food items in 373 adult common dolphinfish examined off North Carolina; the Figure 8 caption attributes the chart to Rose (1966), figure 26. The original Rose thesis was not independently reviewed.

A separate Gulf Stream stomach-content sample of 46 common dolphinfish reported multiple fish and invertebrate groups but no flyingfish, showing that the North Carolina figure is not a fixed universal diet ratio.
The synopsis states that diet changes during growth and summarizes larval crustacean/copepod feeding; do not flatten life-stage and regional variation into one fixed menu.
This secondary synthesis does not verify the cited prey relation in Batanes and does not support local bait recommendations, catchability, occurrence, or a public-app diet assertion.
